rv.q: It’s both a love letter to film-making and a searching study of how to live a good life amid all of its difficulties.
It’s funny, quirky and poignant too, because Ian Shaw is playing his own father.
The two others on the boat are newcomer Richard Dreyfuss – a top impression from Liam Murray Scott – and the great Roy Scheider as police chief Brody, benevolently played by Demetri Goritsas.
It’s a theatrical-cinematic stroke of genius.
Shaw Jr is absolutely spellbinding in his delivery of a warts-and-all eulogy to his long-lost old man.
Demetri Goritsas, as Scheider, has what Shaw called 'the look of incorruptibility'.
Shaw Jr comes close to cartooning his dad's gruff, narrow-eyed delivery and his romanticised grit, but in the end his performance feels respectful.

All of which is amusing to witness even if it never feels especially incisive in its observations about human weakness, male egos and relationships between men who are never sure if they're comrades or rivals.
The delayed West End transfer is a genuine treat for fans of the movie, as it gleefully uncovers facts about the filming.
The result lacks tension, given structure only by the passing of time and the thawing of relations between its cast.
Slickly directed by Guy Masterson, it’s revealing and richly funny.
But, ultimately, it fails to stay afloat.
Mesmerising performances, an immaculate script and a larger but suitably claustrophobic venue make this one of the must-sees of the year.
This is a highly original 90 minutes, packed with wit, insight and pop culture references.
There is nothing faulty about The Shark is Broken; it is theatre well worth seeing.
Thanks to the writing and performances there are plenty of laughs on offer here.
From its initial promising conceit, the script’s gradual decline in tension feels all the more noticeable given that masterly control of tension is the quality that distinguishes the original film.
The Shark is Broken has a freewheeling quality ready-made for Festival high spirits after a pint or two.
The play is a funny and occasionally touching account of the behind-the-scenes shenanigans.
Strong writing and astute performances makes this a superb addition to the West End, and is a fascinating look below the surface of Spielberg’s Hollywood hit.
The Shark is Broken is a standalone piece; you don’t need to have any prior knowledge of Jaws to be able to enjoy it.
Forget pantomime – theatregoers would do well to celebrate a post-Covid Christmas by taking themselves to the Ambassadors Theatre this Christmas instead.

cn.t: Critics praise Ian Shaw's mesmerizing performance as his father in this witty behind-the-scenes Jaws comedy, though some find it occasionally struggles to sustain its premise beyond Edinburgh Fringe charm.
